name: StaticPush by Quintaphon
author: Quintaphon

sections.description:
StaticPush by Quintaphon is a static site generator for WordPress. It exports your WordPress site to plain HTML and publishes it to GitHub (for Cloudflare Pages or any Git-based host), straight to Cloudflare Pages, or as a ZIP. After the first full push, every change you make in WordPress is pushed automatically, and only the pages that changed are sent.

Your visitors get a static site: fast, cheap to host and with nothing to hack. You keep editing in WordPress as usual.

Plugin site: quintaphon.com/wordpress/staticpush
Documentation: quintaphon.com/docs/wordpress/staticpush

Publish

  • Destinations: GitHub (one-click “Connect GitHub”, repository picker, create a repository), Cloudflare Pages Direct Upload, or a local folder and ZIP download.
  • Automatic pushes: on publish, update, unpublish, delete, comments, terms and site-wide changes (menus, widgets, Customizer, theme). Edits made close together become one push.
  • Push only what you need: pending changes, the full site, the current files, or specific pages (including the 404 page).
  • Fast exports: several pages are fetched at once, directly from your own server.
  • Safe by design: a push that would delete most of the static site is refused, and a login wall in front of WordPress stops the push instead of emptying the site.
  • Scheduled posts: overdue scheduled posts are published and pushed, even though the WordPress install gets almost no visitors.

Export

  • Full address or root-relative links, with every occurrence rewritten (including inline CSS, scripts and JSON).
  • Finds everything through the WordPress database and by following links: posts, pages, custom post types, categories, tags, authors, pagination, feeds, sitemaps, robots.txt and ads.txt, and the 404 page.
  • The theme’s real 404 page, marked noindex.
  • Feeds saved as feed.xml with a readable browser view, and old feed addresses redirected.
  • Sitemaps with a readable browser view, and /sitemap.xml redirected to the sitemap index.
  • Additional pages, files and folders; excluded addresses.
  • Renamed posts and pages: the old address 301-redirects to the new one automatically (also for posts renamed earlier). Renamed categories and tags redirect to their new address; deleted ones to their parent category or the homepage.
  • Cloudflare Pages _redirects and _headers (including rules from the Redirection plugin and Yoast, Rank Math, AIOSEO and SEOPress sitemaps).

Features for the static site

  • Site Search: a search index and an instant search overlay that takes over your theme’s search forms. Fuzzy, typo-tolerant matching with Fuse.js, bundled and self-hosted.
  • llms.txt for AI tools: a Markdown summary of the site at /llms.txt (llmstxt.org format) with your categories, pages and latest posts, rebuilt on every push.
  • Related Posts: built into every post at export time, matched by shared tags or categories (topped up with the latest posts when few match), in the Jetpack Related Posts design, a simple grid or your own template.
  • Forms: remove comment forms, or send POST forms to an external form service.
  • HTML Clean-up: add a main landmark for accessibility when the theme has none; remove HTML comments, sourceURL markers, block editor and emoji styles, Dashicons, admin-bar CSS, Yoast schema, speculation rules and more; resource hints; HTML minify; your own removal rules.
  • Stealth: Private WordPress mode hides the WordPress hostname from visitors and search engines while exports keep working; generator tags and WordPress API links can be removed.

Media Offload

Mirror your media library to a Cloudflare R2 bucket over the S3 API: resumable background sync with parallel uploads, pause and resume, automatic upload of new media, skip rules for sizes you don’t need, and media links in exported pages pointed at your media domain. Image sizes kept out of R2 are replaced by the original in exported pages, so no image breaks.

Monitor

  • Dashboard with live progress, push history and an activity log.
  • Health Check: permalinks, loopback requests, background worker, direct fetch, WP-Cron, PHP, disk space, destination connection and more.
  • WP-CLI: wp static-push export [--no-deploy], wp static-push deploy, wp static-push status, wp static-push cancel.

External services

StaticPush by Quintaphon connects to the external services below. Each one is used only for a feature you turn on and set up yourself; with none of them set up, the plugin only writes the static files to a folder on your server (Local / ZIP). No data is sent to Quintaphon.

GitHub

What it is for: connecting your GitHub account and publishing the static site to a repository you choose (Destination: GitHub).

What is sent and when:

  • When you click Connect GitHub: the plugin’s public OAuth client ID is sent to github.com (/login/device/code), and the device code to /login/oauth/access_token while you approve access on github.com. Your GitHub user name is then read from api.github.com.
  • When you open the Destination page or pick a repository: your access token is sent to api.github.com to list your repositories, or to create one when you click New.
  • When a push runs: the exported files and their paths, the commit message and your access token are sent to api.github.com.

GitHub Terms of Service and Privacy Statement.

Cloudflare Pages

What it is for: publishing the static site straight to a Cloudflare Pages project (Destination: Cloudflare Pages, Direct Upload).

What is sent and when: when you save or test the Destination settings, create a project, or a push runs, your Cloudflare account ID, API token and project name are sent to api.cloudflare.com. During a push, the exported files, their paths and content hashes are sent to create the deployment.

Cloudflare Terms of Service and Privacy Policy.

Cloudflare R2

What it is for: storing a copy of your media library in your own R2 bucket (Media Offload).

What is sent and when: only when Media Offload is turned on. When you test the connection, run Sync media library, remove skipped files, or upload new media (with automatic upload on), your media files and their paths are sent to your bucket at <account id>.r2.cloudflarestorage.com (or the S3 endpoint you enter), signed with your R2 access keys.

Cloudflare Terms of Service and Privacy Policy.

Form service you choose (optional)

What it is for: making forms work on the static site, where WordPress can’t receive them.

What is sent and when: only if you enter a form endpoint under Forms. The exported pages then send the form to that address (for example Formspree) from the visitor’s browser when the visitor submits a form. The plugin itself sends nothing. The data is whatever the form contains, and the terms and privacy policy of the service you choose apply (for Formspree: Terms and Privacy Policy).

No other external requests are made. The static site’s search script and Fuse.js are served from your own site, and the admin screens load no files from other sites.

Third-party libraries

  • Fuse.js 7.5.0, Apache License 2.0 (assets/vendor/LICENSE-fuse.txt). The bundled file is the official minified build; the readable source is at https://github.com/krisk/Fuse (tag v7.5.0).
  • Inter variable font 4.x (latin, latin-ext), SIL Open Font License 1.1 (assets/fonts/OFL.txt). Used by the admin screens only. Source: https://github.com/rsms/inter

Developer hooks

Filters: cfsp_full_urls, cfsp_post_urls, cfsp_exclude_url, cfsp_rewrite_content, cfsp_clean_html, cfsp_fetch_args, cfsp_post_types, cfsp_github_client_id, cfsp_github_protected, cfsp_github_allow_mass_delete.

Actions: cfsp_job_done, cfsp_job_failed, cfsp_settings_updated.
sections.installation:
1. Install StaticPush by Quintaphon from Plugins > Add New (or upload the zip) and activate it.
  2. Go to Static Push > Destination, choose GitHub and click Connect GitHub. Enter the code shown on github.com and approve.
  3. Pick a repository, or click New to create a private one.
  4. Go to Export > Link rewriting, choose Full address and enter your public site address (for example https://www.example.com). Save.
  5. Click Push > Full site.
  6. In Cloudflare: Workers & Pages > Create > Pages > Connect to Git, pick the repository. Framework preset: None, build command: empty, output directory: /.

From now on every change in WordPress becomes a commit, and Cloudflare Pages publishes it.

Recommended: move WordPress to its own hostname (for example wp.example.com), point your public domain at the static host, and turn on Stealth > Private WordPress.

Media on Cloudflare R2 (optional): create a bucket and an R2 API token with Object Read & Write, enter them under Media Offload, click Test connection, then Sync media library now. Connect your media domain to the bucket (R2 > bucket > Settings > Custom Domains) and run a full push.

Keys can also live in wp-config.php instead of the database:

define( 'CFSP_GITHUB_TOKEN', 'github_pat_...' );  // fine-grained token for one repository
define( 'CFSP_API_TOKEN', '...' );                // Cloudflare Pages Direct Upload
define( 'CFSP_ACCOUNT_ID', '...' );
define( 'CFSP_R2_ACCESS_KEY', '...' );            // Media Offload
define( 'CFSP_R2_SECRET_KEY', '...' );
define( 'CFSP_BASIC_AUTH', 'user:password' );     // if WordPress is behind HTTP basic auth
sections.faq:
Do I need to keep WordPress running?

Yes. You keep writing and editing in WordPress; Static Push turns the result into a static site. Visitors only ever see the static copy, so WordPress can live on a private hostname.

How long does a full push take?

It depends on the number of addresses (posts, category and tag pages, pagination, feeds, files) and on how fast WordPress builds a page. A site with a few thousand addresses usually takes 10 to 20 minutes. After that, automatic pushes only export the pages that changed.

Will comments, contact forms and search work?

Search works through the built-in static search. Forms can be sent to an external form service. WordPress comments need WordPress, so remove the comment form or use an external comments service.

My scheduled posts are published late.

WP-Cron only runs when someone visits WordPress. Keep Automation > Publish missed scheduled posts on, and have a service such as cron-job.org call the wp-cron.php address shown on that page every minute.

What happens to my data if I delete the plugin?

By default, settings, the GitHub connection, media records and exported files are kept, so reinstalling picks up where you left off. Turn on Tools > Delete all data when the plugin is deleted first if you want everything removed. Your static site, GitHub repository and R2 bucket are never touched.

Does it work with page caches?

Yes. Exports bypass page caches with a query parameter and a no-cache header.
sections.changelog:
2.16.8

  • Fix: when a post was taken out of a category or tag, automatic pushes refreshed only the archives of the terms it still had, so the old category page on the static site kept listing the post until the next full export. The archive (and its feed) of every removed category or tag is now pushed too. The same applies to the old author page when the author changes, and to the old date archives when the publish date moves to another month.

2.16.7

  • The generated site and work files now live in one folder, uploads/staticpush, kept from direct web access: deny rules for Apache and IIS, an empty index, and random per-site sub-folder names that also protect them on nginx. Existing folders are moved there automatically the first time no push is running; files keep their dates, so nothing is uploaded again.
  • The feed and sitemap page script tag is now built with wp_get_script_tag().

2.16.5

  • When Cloudflare refuses a request without an error list, the log now shows the start of its reply, so the cause is visible.

2.16.4

  • Folder locations (site folder, uploads, themes, plugins) now come from WordPress functions, so exports work when wp-content or uploads are moved.
  • The core sitemap address comes from get_sitemap_url().

2.16.3

  • The plugin is now licensed under the GNU General Public License, version 2 or later, ready for the WordPress.org plugin directory.

2.16.2

  • Change: feeds and sitemaps no longer use XSLT stylesheets. Chrome now shows “This site uses XSLT; that functionality is being removed from this browser very soon” on them, and other browsers are dropping XSLT too. Instead each feed and sitemap gets one script tag (rss-style.js, main-sitemap.js) that turns the XML into a readable page in a browser, with clickable links, in the same design as before. Feed readers and search engines ignore the tag.
  • Change: the SEO plugin’s own XSLT stylesheet line is now removed from sitemaps, and WordPress’s from feeds, even with the browser view switched off.
  • Change: the “Custom rss-style.xsl” and “Custom main-sitemap.xsl” boxes are replaced by “Extra CSS” boxes for the feed and sitemap pages. A custom XSL saved earlier is no longer used.
  • Note: run one “Full site” push (or push the feed and sitemap addresses) after updating, so every feed and sitemap is exported again. Old rss-style.xsl and main-sitemap.xsl files on the static site are left in place.

2.15.10

  • Fix: on sites with a very large export folder the Static Push page could stop loading part-way (blank page, no menu links working), because the “Exported files” count loaded every exported file into memory. The count is now taken without holding the file list, is cached for five minutes, and skips folders that cannot be read instead of failing.

2.15.9

  • New: Automation > “Refresh listing pages up to” (0 by default, which keeps the old behaviour). On sites with many posts, one new or removed post moves every older post down a place, so an automatic push re-exported every page 2, 3 and so on of the home page and its categories (over 1,300 pages on a site with 53,000 posts). Set a page number to refresh only up to that page; later pages are brought up to date by the next full export. Pushes of specific pages still refresh every page.

2.15.8

  • Fix: links written with the static site’s own address (the Destination URL, with or without “www.”) were treated as external, so images and files linked that way in posts were never exported by partial or automatic pushes, and only reached the static site through a full push with “Every uploaded file” on. They are now read as the same WordPress address and exported like any other internal link. Nothing changes when no Destination URL is set.

2.15.7

  • Fix: a wildcard line in the _redirects box (for example “/page/* / 301”) could silently switch off most other redirects. Cloudflare Pages counts every line after the first wildcard (* or :placeholder) rule toward its limit of 100 wildcard rules, so renamed-post redirects, feed redirects and /sitemap.xml further down stopped working. Plain rules are now always written before wildcard rules, each group keeping its order.
  • The activity log warns when _redirects has more rules than Cloudflare Pages applies (2,000 plain, 100 wildcard).

2.15.6

  • Fix: on some servers every exported page could come out empty (only the search script tag was left), which published a blank static site. The “Remove emoji scripts & styles” clean-up used a pattern that runs out of PCRE stack (“JIT stack limit exhausted”) on pages with large inline scripts, and PHP then returns nothing instead of the page. The emoji and admin-bar clean-ups now check each script or style block separately, which stays within PCRE limits on any page size.
  • Safer exports: if any clean-up or link-rewrite pattern fails on a page, that one step is skipped and logged, and the rest of the page is kept as it was.
  • Safety net: a page that comes out of processing empty or cut off (its is gone) is no longer saved or pushed. The error is logged and the version from the last push stays on the static site. The 404 page falls back to the built-in one in the same case.

2.15.5

  • Fix: with the Jetpack design, the Related Posts “Headline” setting was ignored on pages that already have Jetpack’s related posts box, so the static site showed Jetpack’s own heading (“Related”). The setting now replaces the heading in Jetpack’s box, keeping its markup and styles. Leave it empty to keep Jetpack’s heading. Run a “Full site” push to update existing pages.
  • Faster full exports on large sites: posts that share the same categories and tags now share one related posts lookup for the whole job, instead of running one scoring query per post. The newest posts used to fill short lists, and each related post’s details, are looked up once per batch, and excerpts are only built when they are shown.
  • Much faster site search index on large sites. It is rebuilt at the end of every push, including small automatic ones, and used to read every post in full (content and custom fields) in pages of 300, re-sorting the whole posts table for each page. It now reads only the title, address and date of each post, in one sorted list (content is still read when “Show excerpts” is on). On a site with 50,000 posts this took a one-page push from about 4.5 minutes to seconds.
  • The activity log now ends each export with a timing summary: time spent waiting for WordPress to render pages, processing pages (and related posts), and job bookkeeping.

2.15.4

  • Fix: when a post split into pages with the Page Break block () was updated, automatic and “Pending changes” pushes re-exported only its first page, so page 2, 3 and onward kept the old content on the static site. All pages of the post are now exported. Run one “Full site” push after updating to refresh pages that are already out of date.

2.14.9

  • First public release.
